title: Other people's things: -ning and two-noun phrases
goal: Show possession when the owner isn't a pronoun, and link two nouns into one term — a pattern you've already met in *metro bekati* in unit 8.
bekal: telling phrases with *-ning* apart from phrases without it

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Bu kimning sumkasi?
dialogs.intro: A bag has been left behind in the classroom. Nilufar, Budi, and Anvar gather around it.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Bilmayman. Mening sumkam qora, bu esa jigarrang.
lines.id: I don't know. My bag is black, but this one is brown.
lines.literal: know-not-I. my bag-my black, this as-for brown.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.text: Ichida nima bor? Balki egasining ismi bordir.
lines.id: What's inside? Maybe the owner's name is there.
lines.literal: inside-its-in what exists? maybe owner-its-'s name-its exists-probably.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Ochaman... Bitta daftar va universitetning kartasi.
lines.id: I'll open it... A notebook and a university card.
lines.literal: open-I... one notebook and university-'s card-its.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.id: I know Dilnoza! She's my sister's classmate.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Great. Then give the bag to her.

lines.speaker: Anvar:
lines.text: Uning telefon raqami menda bor. Hozir yozaman.
lines.id: I have her phone number. I'll text her now.
lines.literal: her phone number-its me-at exists. now write-I.

lines.speaker: Nilufar:
lines.text: Tez boʻling, darsning boshlanishiga besh daqiqa qoldi.
lines.id: Hurry, class starts in five minutes.
lines.literal: quick be, lesson-'s start-its-to five minute remained.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Let's hurry! I hope the classroom door isn't closed yet.

notes: **Kimning sumkasi? — two markers for one possession.** The owner gets *-ning*, the thing gets *-i*. English marks only one side ("whose bag", "Anvar's book"); Uzbek marks both. Drop either one and the sentence feels lopsided.

**Sinf eshigi, without -ning.** Compare *darsning boshlanishi*, which uses it. The difference is explained in the second grammar section: phrases naming a **type** drop *-ning*, phrases naming a **specific owner** keep it.

**Balki … -dir expresses a guess.** *Balki bordir* = "maybe there is". The ending *-dir* goes on the end and means "probably, perhaps". Don't mix it up with the causative *-dir* found in words like *kuldirmoq* (to make laugh).

**Egasi = its owner.** From *ega* (owner). Note that it already has a possessive ending and still gets *-ning* on top: *egasining ismi* = "the name of its owner". Uzbek endings really can stack that deep, and the order never changes.

grammars.title: -ning + -i: the full possessive pattern
body: This follows straight on from unit 3. There the owner was a pronoun; here the owner is a noun or a person's name.
after: Note that the ending on the thing is exactly the third-person possessive from unit 3: *-i* after a consonant, *-si* after a vowel. You're not learning a new rule, just using the old one with a new owner.
⚠️ Words that dropped a vowel in unit 3 do it again here: *eshik* → *eshi**g**i* (k softens to g), *shahar* → *shahri*, *ogʻiz* → *ogʻzi*.
To answer "whose is it?" without repeating the thing, use *-niki*: *Bu sumka kimniki?* — *Dilnozaniki.* The *-niki* form goes straight onto the name, without *-ning*.

grammars.title: When -ning is dropped
body: Uzbek has two kinds of two-noun phrases, and the difference matters. The question is: **does the first word name a specific owner, or a type?**
after: **Look at the last row: both are correct, but they mean different things.** *Sinf eshigi* is a type of door (a classroom door, not a bedroom door). *Sinfning eshigi* is the door belonging to the particular classroom you're talking about.
The good news: **the -i ending on the second word is always there**, with or without *-ning*. If in doubt, keep *-i* and drop *-ning* — it almost always sounds natural.
This pattern without *-ning* builds most Uzbek compound terms: *ish kuni* (workday), *tugʻilgan kun* (day of birth → birthday), *Oʻzbekiston poytaxti* (the capital of Uzbekistan).

sections.title: On campus and at the office

blocks.text: Vocabulary that almost always appears as two-noun phrases — the most natural place to practice this unit's pattern.

⚠️ *Til* means both **tongue and language** — just like "mother tongue" in English, or *language* coming from Latin *lingua* (tongue). The form *oʻzbekcha* from unit 6 is more everyday; *oʻzbek tili* is more formal and used in course names.
Useful for describing the people you talk about — and all of them, as usual, stand in front of the noun without changing form.

Note the ending **-li** in *aqlli*: it means "having", so *aql* (mind) + *-li* = "smart". Its partner *-siz* means "without": *aqlsiz* (foolish), *pulsiz* (without money), *ishsiz* (unemployed). The same two endings you met in *goʻshtli* and *goʻshtsiz* in unit 13.
⚠️ *Keksa* is for people, *eski* for things. Calling a person *eski* sounds like calling them secondhand junk — an easy mistake, since English uses one word, "old", for both.
